name: Fastow (Enron): one question left, strong interview
description: A near-complete, thorough interview of Andrew Fastow (about 175 questions) that follows Dakota's interview outline: the full Upjohn warning with a check of his understanding, how the interview will go and ground rules, open invitations on each topic in chronological order, LJM1 and the Board representation locked in, Chewco, LJM2 controls and late-signed approvals, the Raptor returns, Southampton Place, the 2001 Chewco buyout and tax payment, documents identified and authenticated before use, follow-up on vague answers, certainty and how he knows, other witnesses and what they'd know, and his personal records. Only the final closing question is left. Ask it, then End & grade.
expert_role: Executive Vice President and CFO, Enron Corp.
resume_hint: Ask the last question, then click End & grade: "Thank you. Please keep all related documents and notes, keep today confidential, and don't discuss it with other witnesses. We may follow up. Anything to add or correct?" If his answer opens something new (for example, he corrects an earlier answer), follow it up before ending: ask him to tell you everything he remembers about it, then who, what, when, and how he knows.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Good morning. Andy Fastow. Nobody's told me much about what this is, so I assume you'll fill me in.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Good morning, Mr. Fastow. Thank you for coming in. My name is Jordan Reyes. The Special Investigative Committee of Enron's Board has retained us to investigate the LJM and Chewco transactions and related concerns that have been raised at the company. The purpose of our interview today is to learn the facts so we can give legal advice to the company. To be clear, we represent the Committee and the company only. We do not represent you personally, we are not your attorney, and we can't give you legal advice. This interview is confidential and privileged, but that privilege belongs to the company, not to you or to us. The company decides whether to waive it, and it may disclose what we learn, including to the government, without your consent and without telling you. It's still important that you are fully open and truthful with us, and that you don't share the substance of this interview with anyone. Do you understand? Do you have any questions?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: That's clear, thank you. I understand you're not my lawyer. I may want my own counsel involved at some point, but I'm comfortable talking today. Go ahead.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Before we go on, could you tell me in your own words your understanding of who we represent, and who controls the privilege?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: You represent the Committee and the company, not me. The company controls the privilege and can share what I tell you, without asking me.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Thank you. You're free to consult your own lawyer at any time, and if you'd like to stop to do that, just tell me. As I said, we can't advise you on that. Let me explain how today will go. I'll start with your background and role, then ask you to walk me through the LJM and Chewco transactions in your own words, and later I'll show you some documents. Please give me complete answers, even if a detail seems minor. A few ground rules: if you're speculating, assuming, or estimating, please tell me. Throughout, please tell me whether you actually remember something or are reconstructing it, and say so if you're unsure. And if a question is unclear, ask me to clarify. Is that all right?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: That's fine. I'll tell you if I'm guessing.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Let's start with your role. As CFO, what were you responsible for?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Financing the company: raising capital, managing the balance sheet, and our structured finance work.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What did the Global Finance group do?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: It found partners and investors for our assets and handled hedging. We were growing quickly, and my job was to make sure the money kept up with the business.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who reported to you in Global Finance in 1999 and 2000?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: A good number of people. Ben Glisan, who became Treasurer in 2000. Michael Kopper, a managing director. And a team of deal people under them.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What was Michael Kopper's role?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Michael ran structured transactions for me. He worked on the partnership deals, among other things.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Tell me everything you remember about how LJM1 came about in 1999.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Enron had a big gain in Rhythms NetConnections stock that we couldn't sell, and Jeff Skilling wanted it protected. Nobody in the market would hedge a position like that. So Ben Glisan and I designed a vehicle with outside equity that could use value sitting in some Enron stock forward contracts to hedge the Rhythms position. That became LJM.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Why did you need to be the general partner, rather than someone outside Enron?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: The investors needed someone who understood Enron's assets and could move fast. Frankly, my involvement is what made outside money comfortable. I didn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What do you mean when you say your involvement made outside money comfortable?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Investors trusted that I knew the assets and could get deals done with Enron.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Did your position at Enron play a part in getting investor commitments?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: My knowledge of Enron did, certainly. That's why I was valuable to them.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who first suggested that you serve as the general partner?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I raised it with Ken Lay and Jeff Skilling around the middle of June 1999. I presented it as something the deal needed rather than something I wanted, and they agreed to take it to the Board.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Tell me about the June 28, 1999 Board meeting. What did you present?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Project LJM: the partnership with outside equity, the Rhythms hedge, and the value to Enron. The Board also had to approve a waiver under the Code of Conduct because of my role.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What did you tell the Board about how you personally would be compensated by LJM?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: That I would put in a million dollars of my own money as general partner and would not receive any current or future value from the Enron stock in the partnership.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: At the time, what was your understanding of whether you personally would benefit from the value of the Enron stock held by LJM?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: That I wouldn't. The structure said the general partner wouldn't get any current or future value of the Enron stock.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Next, I'd like to cover the Rhythms unwind in early 2000. Tell me everything you remember about how the hedge was unwound.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Rick Causey came to me and said the company wanted to unwind it. I told him I'd negotiate with the limited partners, and we reached terms in March 2000. Causey's team reviewed them and found them fair.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who negotiated the unwind for Enron?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Causey's group.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who negotiated it for LJM?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I handled it, along with Michael Kopper.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Did anyone at Enron raise concerns with you at the time about your negotiating for LJM?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Everyone knew my role. That's what the Board approval and the controls were for. Causey's people did their own review. I don't recall anyone objecting.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: When you say Causey's people did their own review, who specifically reviewed the unwind terms?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Rick Causey's accounting group. I don't remember the individual names. Rick would know.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who in Mr. Causey's group would we talk to?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I'd start with Rick himself. His staff would know who worked on the unwind.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Let's turn to Chewco. Tell me everything you remember about how Chewco came to be formed in 1997.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: We needed to buy out CalPERS' interest in JEDI so CalPERS would invest in a larger partnership, and we needed an outside buyer to keep JEDI off the balance sheet. Chewco was set up to buy that interest.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who managed Chewco?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Michael Kopper.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Why Mr. Kopper rather than you?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Michael was well suited to it. There were various considerations at the time.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What were those considerations?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Our lawyers advised that if a senior officer like me took part, it would have to be disclosed in the proxy statement and approved under the Code of Conduct. Michael wasn't a senior officer, so neither applied.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Was one aim of choosing Mr. Kopper to avoid that disclosure?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: The aim was to get the deal done efficiently. Avoiding a proxy disclosure was part of that, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who at Enron knew that Mr. Kopper was involved in Chewco?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Jeff Skilling approved it. I believe he told the Board.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: How do you know Mr. Skilling told the Board?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I don't know that personally. That was my understanding.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Were you on the Executive Committee call on November 5, 1997, when Chewco was presented?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I believe so, yes.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Did anyone on that call mention Mr. Kopper's role in Chewco?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I don't recall it coming up specifically.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Is there anything that would help you remember, such as notes, minutes, or a presentation from that call?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: There would have been minutes. I'd defer to those.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who else was on that call?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: The Executive Committee members, Jeff Skilling, and Michael, I believe.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who presented Chewco on that call?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I gave the presentation, I believe. Michael was on the line.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What else was happening around that time that might help you place the call?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: We were trying to close the CalPERS buyout by year end. I still don't recall Michael's role being discussed.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: I'd like to show you the minutes of the November 5, 1997 Executive Committee meeting. Do you recognize them?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: They look like the Committee's minutes from that call.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who prepared them?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: The Corporate Secretary's office prepared the minutes.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Do they help you remember whether Mr. Kopper's role came up?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: They don't mention Michael, which fits my memory that it didn't come up.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Do you recall how Chewco was described on that call, for example whether it was affiliated with Enron?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I believe it was described as an outside entity, not affiliated with Enron or CalPERS. That was the structure.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What was your understanding of whether Chewco was affiliated with Enron?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: It wasn't, as far as I was concerned. Michael wasn't acting for Enron there. He was investing on his own account.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: I'd like to turn to LJM2 and the controls around it. Tell me everything you remember about the controls put in place when the Board approved LJM2 in October 1999.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Every LJM2 transaction had to be approved by Rick Causey and Rick Buy, and the Audit Committee reviewed the LJM2 transactions every year. They were strong controls.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: How do you know they reviewed every transaction?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: That was the requirement. I assumed it was followed. I didn't check each one myself.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: How did those reviews work in practice? Take a specific deal.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: There was an approval sheet for each deal, and the deal team brought it forward. Causey and Buy signed off.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Take Raptor I. What did Mr. Causey and Mr. Buy actually review before they signed its approval sheet?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: They had the deal summary and the approval sheet. How deeply they went into the economics was their call, not mine.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: When did they sign it, relative to the closing?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I'd have to look at the sheet. Some approvals were papered after a deal closed. That happened.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Which approvals were signed after closing?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I don't have a list. The LJM2 approval sheet on one of the early deals was signed some weeks after it closed, I believe.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who asked for them to be signed late?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Nobody asked for that specifically. The deal teams moved fast, and the paperwork caught up afterward.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Why were they signed after closing rather than before?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Quarter-end deals had to close on a deadline, and getting every signature in time wasn't always possible.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: How did you learn about the timing?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I saw the signed sheets come back after the deals had closed. I didn't track the dates myself.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: For Raptor I specifically, when did it close?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: In April 2000.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: When was its approval sheet signed?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Some weeks later, I believe. The sheet itself would show the dates.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who signed the Raptor I approval sheet?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Ben Glisan, Rick Causey and Rick Buy. Jeff Skilling's line was left blank, I believe.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: For the Raptor I approval sheet in April 2000, who negotiated for Enron?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Ben Glisan was listed as the person negotiating for Enron, I believe.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who did Mr. Glisan report to at that time?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: To me. But he was perfectly capable of representing Enron's interests.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who on Enron's side reviewed Mr. Glisan's negotiations with LJM2?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Causey and Buy, through the approval sheets.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Turning to the Raptor returns. Tell me what you remember about the return the Board and Finance Committee expected LJM2 to earn on the Raptors.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Around 30 percent, plus fees. That was in the May 2000 presentation.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What returns did LJM2 actually earn on the Raptors?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: The returns were good. I don't have the exact figures in front of me.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Approximately, then. Were they above or below the 30 percent the Board was shown?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Above, on some of them. The early settlements helped.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: How far above, on the best of them?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Significantly. I'd want to see the investor reports before giving a number.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What's your best estimate?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Well over 100 percent on the best one, I'd guess. I'm estimating.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Now I'd like to ask about any personal interests in these transactions. Did you personally have any financial interest in the Rhythms unwind?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: No, not personally.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Did your family, or any entity connected with you, have one?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: My family has a charitable foundation that makes investments from time to time. I'd have to check its records.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What investments connected to LJM1 did the foundation make in early 2000?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: It may have. It was a small amount.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What do you remember about a partnership called Southampton Place?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: It was a small partnership that bought into LJM1. The Foundation invested in it.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: I'm now going to show you a document: a partnership agreement for Southampton Place, dated March 20, 2000. Do you recognize it?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Yes. I've seen it. The Foundation was one of the partners.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: When did you first see it, and what was its purpose?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Around when it was signed, in March 2000. It set up a small partnership that bought part of an existing limited partner's interest in LJM1, at the time of the Rhythms unwind.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who prepared it, and where was it kept?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: LJM1's counsel drafted it. The Foundation kept a signed copy with its records.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Turn to the signature page. Is that the Foundation's signature?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Yes, that's our signature block.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: It lists a $25,000 contribution from the Fastow Family Foundation. Is that the investment you mentioned a moment ago?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Yes. That's the small amount I was referring to.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: What return did the Foundation receive on that investment?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: It did very well.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: How much did it receive?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I'd have to check. A few million.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Our information is that on May 1, 2000, about six weeks after it invested, the Foundation received roughly $4.5 million on its $25,000. Is that accurate?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: It's in that range, yes.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: How certain are you of that figure?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Fairly certain it was around four and a half million.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Which records would show the exact amount?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: The Foundation's account statements would show it.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Earlier you said you told the Board you would not receive any current or future value from the Enron stock in LJM. Is that still your recollection?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Yes, as to my economics as general partner.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: The Foundation received about $4.5 million from an interest tied to the Rhythms unwind. Help me understand how those fit together.

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: The Foundation isn't me, and what I told the Board was about my economics as general partner. This was a separate investment, made later, on market terms.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who makes the Foundation's investment decisions?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: My wife and I.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who decided that the Foundation would invest in Southampton?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I did.

transcript.speaker: user

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: Michael Kopper and I worked them out with the selling limited partner.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: At that point Enron was negotiating the Rhythms unwind with LJM. Who was looking after Enron's interests while you were setting the Southampton terms?

transcript.speaker: expert

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Did you seek approval under the Code of Conduct for the Foundation's investment?

transcript.message: No. I didn't think the Code applied to the Foundation.

transcript.speaker: user

transcript.speaker: user

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: No.

transcript.speaker: user

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: I don't believe it came up.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: So that I have it right: the Board, Mr. Lay, and Mr. Skilling were not told about the Foundation's Southampton investment, as far as you know?

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who else at Enron invested in Southampton Place?

transcript.speaker: expert
transcript.message: A few people. Michael Kopper, through an entity of his. Ben Glisan. Kristina Mordaunt. Maybe one or two others.

transcript.speaker: user
transcript.message: Who were the others?

transcript.message: Who invited them?

transcript.message: Michael handled those.

transcript.speaker: expert

transcript.message: Michael arranged it. I understood it was a thank-you for her LJM work.

transcript.speaker: user

transcript.message: I don't think we got into that.

transcript.message: Did Mr. Glisan ask you about the expected return?
